claims.text: Structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is governed by a uniform lattice-strain distribution.
Atomic-size mismatches among the constituent metals induce a uniform distribution of lattice strain.
Uniform lattice strain stabilizes the crystal structure.
Homogeneous lattice strain reduces local variations in the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and elemental segregation.
A balanced strain distribution minimizes localized strain concentrations.
Localized strain concentrations can trigger nucleation of secondary phases under high thermal loads.
After thermal cycling between 473 K and 1923 K, the nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Thermal cycling will produce only minor changes in defect density relative to the initial state.
Thermal cycling will not produce significant elemental segregation relative to the initial state.
Thermal cycling will not produce significant secondary-phase formation relative to the initial state.
The prediction is expected to hold under controlled thermal profiles and defined atmospheres.
Rapid redox changes, chemical impurities, or substantial changes in the local environment may cause deviations from the predicted stability.
The proposed experiment compares each nanoparticle sample after thermal cycling with its room-temperature, pre-cycling structural and chemical baseline.
Observation of significant phase segregation, secondary phases, or notable loss of elemental uniformity after cycling would falsify the hypothesis.
